# Handover

> Handover prepares owner-run businesses in the United States for sale. For a fixed fee it recasts three years of financials to show true owner earnings, analyses customers and revenue, writes the business's story for buyers, organises a document room, and gives the owner a fix-it list and an indicative value range. Handover is not a business broker: it does not list businesses, speak to buyers, negotiate or take success fees.

- Who it is for: owners of businesses worth up to about $10 million, typically planning to sell or retire within a few years, and business brokers with sellers who are not yet ready to list.
- Price: free online readiness score and free 45-minute review. Sale-Ready Package from $5,000 (business worth under $1M), $10,000 ($1M–$3M) or $15,000 ($3M–$10M). Fixed fee, no percentage of the sale.
- Timing: six to eight weeks, about five hours of the owner's time.
- Confidentiality: Handover deals only with the owner and never contacts staff, customers or suppliers.
- Contact: contact@handoveradvisors.com

## Guides
- [How to prepare a business for sale: a checklist](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/how-to-prepare-a-business-for-sale): Preparing a business for sale means fixing five things before a buyer looks: financial records a buyer can verify, a business that runs without you, a customer base that isn't concentrated, paperwork that transfers cleanly, and a price with evidence behind it. Most of it can be done in three to twelve months.
- [What is seller's discretionary earnings (SDE), and how do you calculate yours?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-sellers-discretionary-earnings): Seller's discretionary earnings (SDE) is the total financial benefit one full-time owner takes from a business in a year. You calculate it by starting with pre-tax profit and adding back the owner's pay, interest, depreciation, and any personal or one-off expenses. Small businesses are usually priced as a multiple of SDE.
- [Add-backs: what buyers will and won't accept](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/add-backs-what-buyers-accept): An add-back is an expense in your books that a new owner would not have to pay, such as your own salary, personal costs run through the business, or a one-off legal bill. Buyers accept add-backs that are documented, clearly personal or clearly one-off. They reject ones that are vague, recurring or needed to run the business.
- [Why small businesses don't sell, and what to fix first](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/why-businesses-dont-sell): Small businesses fail to sell for five main reasons: earnings the buyer can't verify, a business that depends on its owner, a few customers making up most of the revenue, paperwork that won't transfer, and a price with no evidence behind it. All five can be fixed before listing, and the financial records should come first.
- [How long does it take to sell a small business?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/how-long-does-it-take-to-sell-a-small-business): Selling a small business typically takes six to twelve months from listing to closing, and longer for larger businesses. Add three to twelve months of preparation beforehand, and a handover period afterwards. Owners who plan to retire at a set date should start two to three years ahead.
- [The documents buyers and lenders ask for when you sell a business](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/documents-buyers-and-lenders-ask-for): Buyers and lenders ask for three years of financial statements and tax returns, current-year figures, sales by customer, the lease, key contracts, licences, an equipment list, and employee details. Lenders on SBA-backed loans generally insist on three years of business tax returns. Having all of it in one organised folder before listing shortens a sale by weeks.
- [Customer concentration: how much is too much when you sell?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/customer-concentration-how-much-is-too-much): Buyers and lenders start to worry when one customer makes up more than about 20% of revenue, or the top five make up more than half. It doesn't stop a sale, but it usually lowers the price or changes the terms. You can reduce the concern with contracts, a long track record and relationships that go beyond the owner.
- [How to make your business run without you](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/make-your-business-run-without-you): To make a business less dependent on its owner, move three things to your team: customer relationships, day-to-day decisions, and the knowledge of how things are done. Start by taking a two-week break and writing down everything that waited for you. Most owners need six to twelve months to make a visible difference.
- [What is my small business worth?](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/what-is-my-small-business-worth): Most small businesses sell for a multiple of what they earn for their owner. Businesses worth under about $2 million typically sell for around two to three times seller's discretionary earnings, and larger ones for around four times EBITDA or more. Where you land in the range depends on how verifiable, transferable and dependable those earnings are.
- [Selling an HVAC, plumbing or electrical business: what buyers look for](https://handoveradvisors.com/guides/selling-an-hvac-plumbing-or-electrical-business): Buyers of HVAC, plumbing and electrical businesses pay most for recurring service-agreement revenue, a team of licensed technicians who will stay, a business that doesn't depend on the owner's licence or relationships, and clean financials. Private-equity-backed groups are actively buying, but they are selective, and preparation decides who gets the premium.

## Questions and answers
### How do I get my business ready to sell?
Buyers and their lenders look at five things: financial records they can verify, a business that can run without its owner, a customer base that is not concentrated in one or two accounts, operations and paperwork that transfer cleanly, and a price with evidence behind it. Getting ready means fixing the gaps in each before a buyer sees the business. Our free ten-minute readiness score shows you where you stand on all five.

### When should I start preparing?
Ideally six to twelve months before you list, because some fixes, such as moving customer relationships to your team, take time. It is still worth doing if you are about to list, or if your business has been listed for a while without selling.

### What does Handover cost?
The readiness score and a 45-minute review call are free. The Sale-Ready Package is a fixed fee: from $5,000 for a business worth under $1 million, from $10,000 for $1 million to $3 million, and from $15,000 for $3 million to $10 million. Half is due when we start and half when we hand back. We never take a percentage of your sale.

### What do I get for that?
Three years of financials recast to show true owner earnings, a customer and revenue analysis, the written story of your business for buyers, an organised document room, a fix-it list ranked by value, and an indicative value range for today and with the gaps closed.

### How long does it take?
Six to eight weeks from kick-off to hand-back, and about five hours of your time: gathering documents, one ninety-minute conversation, and checking the facts in what we write.

### Are you business brokers?
No. We do not list businesses, find or speak to buyers, negotiate, or take success fees. We prepare the business and its documents, and you then sell it through the broker of your choice, or on your own. We also do not give formal valuations, or tax or legal advice.

### What are recast financials?
Most small-business books are kept to keep tax down, so they understate what the business really earns. Recasting restates three years of results to show true owner earnings (often called seller’s discretionary earnings, or SDE), by adding back the owner’s above-market pay, personal expenses run through the business and one-off costs. Each adjustment is tied to a document, so a buyer’s accountant and a bank can rely on it.

### Will anyone find out I am thinking of selling?
No. We deal only with you. We never contact your staff, customers, suppliers or competitors, and nothing you share leaves us without your say-so.

### What size of business do you work with?
Owner-run businesses worth up to about $10 million, in any industry. Most of the owners we work with have run their business for twenty years or more.
